title: 8 How does worker bees form a new queen bee? (part 2)
source: science (1) — 8 How does worker bees form a new queen bee?, pages 17-20 [science (1).pdf]
textbookText: Pupa Stage: At the end of the larval stage, worker bees seal the cell with wax. Inside the sealed cell, the larva spins a cocoon around itself and transforms into a pupa. In this stage, metamorphosis takes place where the larva gradually develops into an adult honey bee. The pupal stage lasts for seven to ten days, depending on the caste of bee. Adult Stage: Finally, the fully developed adult bee emerges from the sealed cell. The time taken to reach adulthood differs among the three types of honey bees: a queen takes about 16 days, a worker takes 21 days, and a drone takes 24 days. Each type has its own role in the colony: the queen lays eggs, workers collect nectar and maintain the hive, and drones fertilize the queen. Fig. Life cycle of Honey 2. Describe the structure of the larva of honey bee with diagram. Ans:- The larva of a honey bee is a small, white, legless, and worm-like organism that hatches from the egg after three days. It has a soft, cylindrical body with a distinct head region but without developed eyes, legs, or wings. The larval body is covered with a thin cuticle and consists of 13 segments. It has chewing mouthparts for feeding on the royal jelly and brood food supplied by worker bees. The larva grows very rapidly, shedding its cuticle (moulting) several times before entering the pupal stage. During this stage, it stores nutrients that are later used for metamorphosis into an adult bee. Worker bees cap the larval cell with wax once it is ready to pupate. 3. Describe the structure of worker bee with diagram. Ans:- The worker bee is the smallest but most active member of a honeybee colony. Its body is divided into three main parts: the head, thorax, and abdomen. The head bears a pair of large compound eyes, three small simple eyes (ocelli), and a pair of antennae that help in smelling, tasting, and sensing vibrations. It also has chewing and lapping type mouthparts, which are useful for collecting nectar, pollen, and building wax combs. The thorax is the center of locomotion and bears two pairs of wings and three pairs of legs. Each pair of legs has a special function: the forelegs help in cleaning the antennae, the midlegs assist in brushing pollen, and the hindlegs are modified with a pollen basket (corbicula) for carrying pollen. The abdomen consists of ten segments and contains important organs and glands. On its underside are wax glands that secrete wax for comb building, and at the tip lies the sting apparatus used for defense. Although the worker bee is female, its reproductive organs are underdeveloped, so it normally does not reproduce. Thus, the worker bee is specially adapted with structures for feeding, defense, and hive maintenance, making it the most hardworking member of the colony. 4. Write the external structure of drone bee with diagram. Ans:- The drone bee is the male member of the honeybee colony. It is larger and stouter than the worker bee but smaller than the queen. The body of the drone is divided into three parts: head, thorax, and abdomen. The head is broad and bears very large compound eyes that almost meet at the top of the head; these help in locating the queen during mating flights. In addition, the head carries a pair of short antennae and simple mouthparts, which are not well developed for collecting nectar or pollen, since drones do not gather food. The thorax is strong and muscular, bearing two pairs of wings and three pairs of legs. Unlike worker bees, the legs of drones are not modified for pollen collection. The abdomen of the drone is blunt at the end and does not have a sting, wax glands, or pollen baskets. Instead, it contains the reproductive organs required for mating with the queen. Thus, the external structure of a drone bee shows adaptations for reproduction rather than for work, and drones usually depend on worker bees for food and survival. 5. Write the functions of worker bee's based on class and age. Ans:- Worker bees perform different duties in the colony according to their age. This age-based division of labor is called polyethism. i) Young Worker Bees (1–3 days old) o Clean the hive and brood cells. o Feed older larvae with diluted honey and pollen.

ii) Nurse Bees (4–10 days old) o Secrete royal jelly from hypopharyngeal glands to feed the queen and young larvae. o Take care of the queen and attend to her needs. iii) Wax-Producing and Comb-Building Bees (11–20 days old) o Secrete wax from wax glands to build and repair combs. o Store nectar and pollen inside the cells. o Guard the hive entrance against intruders. iv) Field or Forager Bees (after 20 days until death) o Collect nectar, pollen, water, and propolis (plant resin). o Communicate food sources to other bees through the waggle dance. o Protect the hive when attacked, using their sting.
